o: We aggregate the ParkingTransactions table per car: total fees, average hourly fee (total fee divided by total hours, rounded to 2 decimals), and the lot where the car accumulated the most parked time. Durations come from TIMESTAMPDIFF between exit and entry. Ordering is by car_id. Since this is a pure SQL problem, one well-structured query solves it.
k: TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, ...) gives exact durations; divide by 3600 for hours.
The most-time lot is a per-group top-1, solvable with a correlated subquery ordered by summed duration.

a.n: Approach 1: Aggregation with a correlated subquery
a.i: First normalize each transaction into (car, lot, fee, duration seconds) in a CTE, then group by car for totals and use a correlated subquery to pick the lot with maximal total duration.
s: Build CTE t computing duration in seconds per row.
Group by car_id: SUM(fee_paid) and ROUND(SUM(fee)/(SUM(dur)/3600), 2).
Correlated subquery groups t2 by lot for the same car, orders by SUM(dur) DESC, takes the first.

c.python:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT car_id, lot_id, fee_paid,
         TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, entry_time, exit_time) AS dur
  FROM ParkingTransactions
)
SELECT car_id,
       SUM(fee_paid) AS total_fee_paid,
       ROUND(SUM(fee_paid) / (SUM(dur) / 3600), 2) AS avg_hourly_fee,
       (SELECT lot_id FROM t t2 WHERE t2.car_id = t.car_id
        GROUP BY lot_id ORDER BY SUM(dur) DESC LIMIT 1) AS most_time_lot
FROM t
GROUP BY car_id
ORDER BY car_id;

a.t: O(T log T) per car group due to the correlated subquery sorting; fine for typical inputs

w: Verify rounding matches expectations (MySQL ROUND is half-away-from-zero for these magnitudes). A pitfall is dividing integer seconds incorrectly — keep the division in floating point. A window-function alternative (ROW_NUMBER over lots by summed duration joined back) also works and scales better if the optimizer struggles with the correlated subquery.
